title: The Good Shepherd and the Feast of Dedication
summary: Jesus describes himself as the gate for the sheep and the good shepherd who knows his sheep by name and lays down his life for them, unlike thieves and hired hands. Months later, at the Feast of Dedication in winter, the authorities demand that he say plainly whether he is the Christ. He answers that his sheep hear his voice and no one can snatch them from his hand, and that he and the Father are one, and they try to stone him for blasphemy before he withdraws across the Jordan.
story:
The chapter follows directly from chapter 9. The Pharisees had thrown a healed man out of the synagogue, and Jesus found him. Now, speaking to the same hearers (compare 9:40 with 10:6 and 10:21), Jesus contrasts the leaders who drive the sheep away with the true shepherd who calls them by name and leads them out. The second half moves ahead to the Feast of Dedication, some two or three months after Tabernacles, and it brings Jesus' public debates in Jerusalem to their peak. The question “If You are the Christ, tell us plainly” (verse 24) is answered with the claim of unity with the Father, and the attempt to stone him shows how near the end has come.

The chapter closes a long section. Since chapter 5 Jesus has been in conflict with the Jerusalem authorities at the feasts: an unnamed feast (5:1), Passover in Galilee (6:4), Tabernacles (7:2), and now Dedication. Each feast has supplied images he claims for himself, bread in the wilderness, water and light at Tabernacles, and here the consecration of the temple. Jesus then withdraws to the place across the Jordan where John the Baptist first baptized (1:28), and the Gospel quietly returns to its beginning, with the Baptist's testimony confirmed (verse 41). The next chapter brings Jesus back toward Jerusalem for the last sign, the raising of Lazarus, which leads to the cross.
historical:
The Feast of Dedication (verse 22), Hanukkah in Hebrew, was not one of the festivals commanded in the law of Moses. It commemorated the rededication of the temple after the Seleucid king Antiochus IV, who called himself Epiphanes, ‘god manifest’, had set up what 1 Maccabees calls the abomination of desolation on the altar on the fifteenth of Kislev in the year 145 of the Seleucid era, 167 BC (1 Maccabees 1:54; compare Daniel 11:31). Judas Maccabeus led a Jewish revolt, recaptured Jerusalem, cleansed the sanctuary, built a new altar, and restored the sacrifices on the twenty-fifth of Kislev, 164 BC. The celebration lasted eight days, and Judas and the assembly decreed that it should be kept every year (1 Maccabees 4:36-59). Second Maccabees says it was kept like the Feast of Tabernacles, with branches and palm fronds and hymns (2 Maccabees 10:1-8), and the letters that open that book call it the days of booths in the month of Kislev (2 Maccabees 1:9). Josephus, writing around AD 93, says the festival was called Lights, and supposes the name came from the unexpected freedom that dawned on the people (Antiquities 12.323-325). The later story of a single cruse of oil that burned for eight days appears in the Babylonian Talmud (b. Shabbat 21b), not in these earlier sources. Kislev falls in November and December, so John's note that it was winter is exact.

The feast celebrated God's deliverance, the purity of the temple, and resistance to a ruler who claimed divine honors. In that setting the question of whether Jesus is the Christ, his claim to be one with the Father, the charge that a man was making himself God (verse 33), and his claim that the Father had consecrated him (verse 36) all carry special weight. The feast remembered a man who called himself god and defiled the temple; the authorities think they face another.

Solomon's Colonnade (verse 23) was the roofed portico along the eastern side of the outer court of Herod's temple, which Josephus says was believed to go back to Solomon (Antiquities 20.220-221; Jewish War 5.184-185). In winter, with the cold wind off the desert to the east, a covered walkway was the natural place to teach; the early church later gathered there (Acts 3:11, 5:12). Stoning was the law's penalty for blasphemy (Leviticus 24:16). The Mishnah, compiled around AD 200, defines blasphemy narrowly as pronouncing the divine Name (m. Sanhedrin 7:5); whatever the first-century rule was, the charge here rests not on a word but on what Jesus claims to be. The hostile questioners are again called the Jews, but the chapter itself reports division among them (verses 19 to 21), and many believe (verse 42). John's usage points to the leaders pressing Jesus in the temple, not the Jewish people as such, a distinction the church too often forgot.
cultural:
Shepherding was an everyday sight in Judea, and the details of verses 1 to 5 are drawn from life. Sheep were kept at night in a fold (aulē), an enclosure with stone walls, sometimes the courtyard of a house, sometimes shared by several flocks, with a gatekeeper at the entrance (verse 3). In the morning each shepherd called his own sheep, which knew his voice, and led them out to pasture, walking ahead of them rather than driving them from behind (verse 4). Shepherds commonly gave their animals names. The Scottish scholar George Adam Smith, traveling in Palestine in the late nineteenth century, reported a shepherd who explained that at night he lay across the open entrance of his fold, so that nothing went in or out except over his body; the story, popularized by William Barclay, illustrates how Jesus could be both shepherd and gate, though it is a modern report, not an ancient source.

The work was dangerous. Jacob speaks of heat by day and frost by night and of losses he had to make good (Genesis 31:38-40). David tells Saul he had struck down lions and bears to rescue lambs (1 Samuel 17:34-35), and Amos pictures a shepherd rescuing two legs or a piece of an ear from a lion's mouth, the proof that the animal was taken and not stolen (Amos 3:12). The law set rules for animals lost while in someone's care (Exodus 22:10-13), and the Mishnah later ruled that a paid shepherd must defend the flock against one wolf, while an attack by two wolves counted as an unavoidable accident (m. Bava Metzia 7:9). The hired hand of verse 12 was not a villain by definition; he simply had limits, and when real danger came he was not expected to die for animals that were not his. That is the contrast Jesus draws.

Across the ancient world kings were called shepherds of their people. Hammurabi calls himself the shepherd in the prologue of his laws, and Homer's heroes are shepherds of the people. Israel's Scriptures use the image for both God and Israel's leaders. Psalm 23 calls the Lord my shepherd, and Isaiah 40:11 pictures him gathering the lambs in his arms. Moses prayed that the Lord's people would not be like sheep without a shepherd and asked for a leader who would go out and come in before them (Numbers 27:17), language Jesus echoes in verse 9. In Ezekiel 34 God condemns Israel's shepherds for feeding themselves and scattering the flock, and promises to shepherd his people himself and to set over them one shepherd, his servant David (Ezekiel 34:23, 37:24). Jeremiah 23:1-6 makes a similar promise, and Zechariah 11 attacks worthless shepherds. The Psalms of Solomon, written around the middle of the first century BC, picture the coming son of David shepherding the Lord's flock faithfully and righteously (Psalms of Solomon 17:40). Jesus' hearers, who had just seen the Pharisees throw out the healed man, would have heard these texts behind his words. The words thief and robber (verses 1 and 8) also had a political edge: lēstēs, robber, is Josephus's regular word for the armed insurgents of the period, and John uses it of Barabbas (18:40).
literary:
The first part (verses 1 to 21) is what John calls a paroimia, a figure of speech (verse 6). It begins with a short parable about a sheepfold, a gate, a gatekeeper, a shepherd, and strangers (verses 1 to 5), and when the hearers do not understand, Jesus unfolds it through two ‘I am’ sayings, the third and fourth of the seven with an image in John: “I am the gate for the sheep” (verse 7, repeated in verse 9) and “I am the good shepherd” (verse 11, repeated in verse 14). Both begin with the double Amen, ‘truly, truly’ (verses 1 and 7). The images shift freely, as they do in Hebrew prophecy, so that Jesus is both the gate and the shepherd, and the parable's thieves become the hired hand and the wolf.

The phrase lay down My life, or its equivalent, comes five times in verses 11 to 18, making the shepherd's death the center of the passage, and it is balanced by take it up again (verses 17 and 18). Verses 14 and 15 set up a chain of knowing: the shepherd knows his sheep and they know him, just as the Father knows the Son and the Son knows the Father. The division in verses 19 to 21 closes the scene by pointing back to chapter 9, with the question whether a demon could open the eyes of the blind.

The second part (verses 22 to 39) is a confrontation that echoes the first. The same words return, sheep, voice, know, follow, give, hand, and life, so that the Dedication dialogue reads as a commentary on the parable. The authorities' demand to be told plainly (parrēsia, verse 24) is met by the claim that Jesus has already told them and that the works testify (verse 25), and the dialogue moves by stages from Christ (verse 24) to one with the Father (verse 30) to Son of God (verse 36) to the Father in me and I in the Father (verse 38). Each claim provokes a stronger response: stones (verse 31), the charge of blasphemy (verse 33), an attempt to seize him (verse 39). The chapter ends with a return to the place where the Gospel's story began with John the Baptist (1:28), closing Jesus' public ministry of teaching in Jerusalem with the verdict of people who had heard the Baptist and now believe (verses 40 to 42).

outline.t: I am the gate for the sheep
I am the good shepherd who lays down his life
At the Feast of Dedication: my sheep hear my voice
An attempt to stone him for blasphemy

doctrines.note: “The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep” (verse 11). The death of Jesus is for others, and it is voluntary: “No one takes it from Me, but I lay it down of My own accord” (verse 18). He dies willingly, under his Father's charge, with authority to take his life up again.

“I and the Father are one” (verse 30). The Greek word for one (hen) is neuter, which points to one in nature and action rather than one person, and the verb are is plural. The church drew on this verse against both those who made the Son a lesser being and those who erased the distinction between Father and Son, and verse 38 adds the mutual indwelling of Father and Son.

Jesus' sheep “will never perish. No one can snatch them out of My hand” (verse 28), and the Father's hand holds them too (verse 29). Christians in the Reformed tradition read this as teaching that true believers are kept to the end; Arminian and other traditions stress that it describes sheep who keep hearing and following (verse 27). All agree that the security of the sheep rests on the shepherd, not on themselves.

“I have other sheep that are not of this fold” (verse 16). Most read this as the gathering of Gentiles with believing Jews into one flock under one shepherd, a gathering John names again in 11:52. The church's unity is grounded in one shepherd, not in one enclosure.

The chapter judges every leader of God's people by the shepherd who lays down his life. Thieves use the sheep, hired hands abandon them, and the good shepherd knows them and dies for them (verses 10 to 15). The New Testament applies the pattern to elders, who shepherd under the chief Shepherd (1 Peter 5:2-4, Acts 20:28).

words.note: Poimēn, shepherd. It occurs eighteen times in the New Testament and six times in John, all in this chapter. In the Old Testament the image covers God, kings, and leaders. When Jesus says “I am the good shepherd,” he steps into the role God promised to take himself in Ezekiel 34. Hebrews calls him the great Shepherd of the sheep (Hebrews 13:20) and 1 Peter the chief Shepherd (1 Peter 5:4). The word later became a title for church leaders (Ephesians 4:11), whose model is the shepherd who gives his life. The hired hand (misthōtos, verses 12 and 13) is his foil.

Kalos, good. It occurs about a hundred times in the New Testament and seven times in John. It can mean morally good, but also noble, beautiful, fitting, or excellent; BDAG lists senses from beautiful to praiseworthy. The good shepherd is the model shepherd, the true and worthy one, as opposed to the hired hand. John uses the same word for the good wine at Cana (2:10) and for the good works Jesus showed from the Father (verses 32 and 33).

Thura, door or gate. It occurs about thirty-nine times in the New Testament and seven times in John, four of them here (verses 1, 2, 7, and 9) and the rest at the high priest's courtyard (18:16) and the locked doors of Easter (20:19, 20:26). Jesus is the entrance to God's flock and its pastures: whoever enters through him will be saved and will come in and go out, the Old Testament idiom for a secure and ordinary life (Deuteronomy 28:6, Psalm 121:8).

Psuchē, life or soul. It occurs about a hundred times in the New Testament and ten times in John. It can mean the inner self, but in the phrase lay down one's life it means a person's very life. John uses the idiom for the shepherd here (verses 11, 15, 17), for Peter's rash promise (13:37-38), and for the greatest love, laying down one's life for friends (15:13); 1 John 3:16 applies it to believers. In verse 24 the same word appears in the idiom how long will you keep our soul in suspense.

Harpazō, to seize or snatch by force. It occurs fourteen times in the New Testament and four in John. The crowd wanted to seize Jesus to make him king (6:15); the wolf snatches the sheep (verse 12); but no one can snatch them from Jesus' hand or from the Father's (verses 28 and 29). The repeated word sets the danger and the protection side by side, and the same verb describes believers caught up to meet the Lord (1 Thessalonians 4:17).

Egkainia, dedication or renewal, from kainos, new. It occurs only here in the New Testament. The Greek Old Testament uses it for the dedication of the rebuilt temple in Ezra's day (Ezra 6:16-17) and of Jerusalem's wall (Nehemiah 12:27), in the heading of Psalm 30 (29 in the Greek numbering), a song for the dedication of the house, and, with a close relative, for Judas's dedication of the altar (1 Maccabees 4:56, 4:59). Here it names Hanukkah. Jesus, speaking of himself as the one the Father consecrated and sent into the world (verse 36), presents himself at this feast as the one truly set apart for God.

Hagiazō, to make holy, consecrate, set apart for God. It occurs about twenty-eight times in the New Testament and four in John: here, and in the prayer of 17:17-19, where Jesus asks the Father to sanctify the disciples and says he sanctifies himself for them. In the Greek Old Testament it is used for consecrating priests, the altar, and the temple (Exodus 29:44, 1 Kings 9:3). At the feast of the altar's reconsecration, Jesus claims to be the one the Father consecrated.

Paroimia, figure of speech, proverb, veiled saying. It occurs five times in the New Testament: four in John (10:6, 16:25 twice, 16:29) and once in 2 Peter 2:22. The Greek title of the book of Proverbs is Paroimiai. John prefers it to parabolē, the Synoptic word for parable. Jesus tells the disciples that he has spoken in figures but that the hour is coming when he will speak plainly (16:25), which answers the authorities' demand for plain speech in verse 24.

christ:
Israel's Scriptures promised a day when God himself would shepherd his scattered people, seek the lost, and bind up the injured, and would raise up one shepherd from David's line to care for them (Ezekiel 34:11-24, 37:24; compare Jeremiah 23:1-6 and Micah 5:4). Jesus claims both roles. He is the good shepherd whose voice the sheep know, and he shares the Father's hand in holding them (verses 28 to 30), so that what Ezekiel promised of the Lord and of David meet in him. He also fulfills the shepherd who is struck: Zechariah 13:7 speaks of the shepherd struck and the sheep scattered, and the other Gospels have Jesus apply it to himself on the night of his arrest (Mark 14:27). Unlike every shepherd before him, he lays down his life for the flock, and he does so in order to take it up again (verses 17 and 18), a clear reference to his death and resurrection.

The promise of other sheep and one flock (verse 16) takes up Ezekiel's one shepherd and the prophets' hope that the nations would be gathered to Israel's God (Isaiah 56:8). John makes the connection himself in 11:52, where Jesus is to die to gather the scattered children of God into one. After the resurrection, the risen shepherd commissions Peter to feed his sheep (21:15-17), and the New Testament speaks of him as the great Shepherd brought back from the dead (Hebrews 13:20), the Shepherd and Overseer of souls (1 Peter 2:25), and the Lamb who will shepherd his people to springs of living water (Revelation 7:17).

At the feast that celebrated a purified temple and a God-given deliverer, Jesus presents himself as the one consecrated by the Father and sent into the world (verse 36). He has already spoken of his body as the temple (2:21). The feast remembered a pagan king who claimed to be god manifest and defiled God's house; John presents the one who truly is one with the Father, who does not seize divine honors but lays down his life. The chapter's claims build to that confession: Christ, one with the Father, Son of God, the Father in him and he in the Father.
interpretation:
The good shepherd became one of the first images of Christ in Christian art. In the Roman catacombs, as early as the third century, a young shepherd carrying a sheep on his shoulders is painted on ceilings in the Catacomb of Callixtus and the Catacomb of Priscilla, and small marble statues of the same figure survive, one of the best known in the Vatican Museums. The figure draws on Luke 15 as well as John 10, and on a pagan type of a shepherd carrying an animal, but Christians read it as Christ. In the Mausoleum of Galla Placidia in Ravenna, from about 450, a mosaic shows Christ as a royal shepherd in gold robes among his sheep, holding a cross.

The fathers used verse 30 in the doctrine of the Trinity. Tertullian (Against Praxeas 22, early third century) observed that Jesus said one thing, not one person, a unity of substance rather than a singularity of number, and so answered those who said the Father and Son were the same. Augustine in his Tractates on John (45 to 48 cover this chapter) made the classic form of the argument: the word one refutes the Arians, who divided the Son's nature from the Father's, and the word are refutes the Sabellians, who erased the persons. John Chrysostom's homilies on John, preached at Antioch around 390, follow the same line. Gregory the Great's homily on the good shepherd (Homilies on the Gospels 14, preached in Rome in 591) turned the passage toward pastors, warning against the hireling who flees when the wolf comes; with his Pastoral Rule (590) it shaped the Western picture of the bishop and pastor for a thousand years.

In the historic Western lectionary John 10:11-16 was read on the second Sunday after Easter, named Misericordias Domini from its opening chant, and Luther and many Lutheran preachers preached on it there. The Roman Catholic calendar and the Revised Common Lectionary keep the chapter on the fourth Sunday of Easter, Good Shepherd Sunday, reading verses 1 to 10, 11 to 18, and 22 to 30 across the three years; since 1964 the Catholic Church has kept it as a day of prayer for vocations. Calvin's commentary (1553) read verses 28 and 29 as a promise of the elect's perseverance, and the Canons of Dort (1619, fifth head) cite the passage in teaching that God preserves true believers to the end. The Remonstrants' fifth article (1610) had left open whether believers could fall away, and later Arminian writers read the promise as conditional on continuing to follow.

Jewish tradition bears on verse 34. The Babylonian Talmud reads Psalm 82:6 as God's word to Israel at Sinai, made like divine beings by receiving the Torah until the sin of the golden calf brought death back (b. Avodah Zarah 5a), and a Qumran text applies Psalm 82:1 to a heavenly Melchizedek who judges (11Q13). Jerome Neyrey (Journal of Biblical Literature 108, 1989) argued that John's use of the psalm draws on this Jewish reading of Israel at Sinai. Modern commentators such as Raymond Brown (Anchor Bible, 1966) connected the Dedication dialogue with the feast's themes of temple and consecration. Latter-day Saints read the other sheep of verse 16 as the Nephites of the Book of Mormon (3 Nephi 15:21); the historic churches read them as Gentiles who would believe.
text:
A few manuscript differences touch this chapter. In verse 7 the early papyrus P75 and the Sahidic Coptic version read ‘I am the shepherd of the sheep’ instead of the gate; almost all other witnesses read gate, and it is clearly original, since it is the harder reading and verse 9 repeats it. In verse 8 some of the oldest witnesses, among them P45, P75, and the first hand of Codex Sinaiticus, lack ‘before Me’, so that the verse reads ‘all who came are thieves and robbers’; other early witnesses, including P66, Vaticanus, and Bezae, have the words, and modern versions keep them. The omission may reflect scribes' worry that the verse condemned Moses and the prophets. In verse 18 Westcott and Hort printed the past tense, ‘no one took it from me’, following some of the oldest manuscripts; the Nestle-Aland text and most versions have the present, ‘no one takes it’. In verse 22 the critical editions read ‘at that time’ (tote) where later manuscripts read ‘and’.

Verse 29 is the chapter's hardest problem. Most manuscripts, with P66, read ‘My Father, who has given them to Me, is greater than all’, which the BSB, ESV, and NIV follow. Codex Vaticanus in its first hand, most of the Latin tradition, and the Bohairic Coptic read ‘what My Father has given Me is greater than all’, and the Nestle-Aland text prints this form; other manuscripts mix the two. The difference in Greek is a single letter in the relative pronoun and one vowel in the word greater. The neuter reading is harder, which may be why scribes changed it, but it makes a strange sense (the flock is greater than all), which is why most translations prefer the easier reading. Either way the promise of verse 28 stands.

One translation difference is well known. In verse 16 the King James Version reads ‘there shall be one fold, and one shepherd’, following the Latin Vulgate's ovile, sheepfold. The Greek has two different words: aulē, fold, earlier in the verse, and poimnē, flock, at its end. Modern versions render one flock, and the difference matters, because the unity Jesus promises is of one flock under one shepherd, not of one enclosure.

teach.big: Jesus is the good shepherd who knows his sheep by name, lays down his life for them of his own will, and holds them in a hand no one can open, because he and the Father are one.

outline.t: The true shepherd comes by the proper way, is recognized by the sheep, and leads them out by name; others use the sheep for themselves.
Jesus is the only gate into God's flock, and those who enter find safety, freedom to come and go, pasture, and life in its fullness.
The good shepherd differs from the hired hand in one thing above all: he knows the sheep and dies for them rather than save himself.
His death gathers other sheep, from outside Israel's fold, into one flock under one shepherd.
Jesus' death is not an accident or a defeat but a free act under his Father's charge, with the resurrection already in view.
The same words that give life to some sound like madness to others, and the healed blind man stands as evidence.
Faith is not a matter of plainer information but of belonging: Jesus' sheep hear him, follow him, and are held by the Son and the Father together.
Jesus answers the charge of blasphemy from Scripture and from his works, and the claim that the Father is in him and he in the Father still divides his hearers.
Away from Jerusalem, people who heard the Baptist find that everything he said about Jesus was true and believe.

teach.pitfalls:
Several misuses recur. The first reads the hired hand of verses 12 and 13 as a weapon against paid ministers, as if drawing a salary made a pastor a hireling. The contrast is between one who owns and loves the sheep and one who abandons them when danger comes, not between paid and unpaid work; Paul defends the support of ministers (1 Corinthians 9:14). The second treats all who came before me as a dismissal of Moses and the prophets. Jesus appeals to Moses and Scripture throughout John (5:46, 10:35); the thieves are those who came claiming to be the shepherd and used the flock, including the leaders of chapter 9.

A third turns verse 10, life in all its fullness, into a promise of health and wealth, when the fullness Jesus gives comes through a shepherd who dies. A fourth takes verse 34, you are gods, as proof that believers are little gods, as some prosperity preachers have taught; Jesus is arguing from Psalm 82 about a title Scripture gave to those who received God's word, not teaching that humans share his divine nature. A fifth uses verses 28 and 29 either to make assurance independent of following Jesus or to deny any real assurance; teachers should state the Reformed and Arminian readings fairly and notice that the verse holds together sheep who follow and a shepherd who keeps. Finally, avoid making the Jews of verses 24 to 33 a picture of Jewish people generally; the chapter reports division, and many believe.
teach.pastoral: This chapter will press hardest on people who have been harmed by religious leaders, those whom pastors used, controlled, or abandoned. Jesus' words about thieves and hirelings are a judgment on that abuse, and it helps to say so plainly; the good shepherd is not the one who hurt them. Teachers who are themselves pastors should let the text judge them first. The chapter also speaks to people troubled by fear that they have fallen away or are not truly among the sheep, a common form of scrupulosity. Point them to the one who holds, not to their own grip, and to the evidence of hearing and following rather than to an introspective search for certainty. And it may touch people who feel like outsiders to the church's fold, for whom the promise of other sheep is good news.

hard.q: When Jesus quotes “I have said you are gods,” is he saying he is divine only in the way others are?
hard.a:
Jesus answers the charge of blasphemy by quoting Psalm 82:6, where God addresses certain beings as gods and sons of the Most High. The strongest form of the objection says that Jesus is backing away from a claim to deity. If Scripture can call mere humans gods, then calling oneself Son of God need mean no more than being a faithful man who has received God's word. Unitarian readers since the Socinians of the late sixteenth century have made this argument, and some modern historical critics hold that the historical Jesus made no claim to divinity and that the Johannine discourses reflect the later church. Jewish readers have noted that in rabbinic tradition the psalm describes Israel at Sinai, made godlike by receiving the Torah (b. Avodah Zarah 5a), so the verse can be read as teaching the high dignity of every faithful Israelite rather than the unique status of one.

Who the psalm's gods are is debated. Many interpreters think it addresses Israel's human judges, who exercised God's authority; Jerome Neyrey (1989) and others argue that John draws on the reading of Israel at Sinai; others think the psalm addresses heavenly beings in God's council, as 11Q13 suggests for Psalm 82:1. On any of these readings, Jesus argues from the lesser to the greater, a form of reasoning the rabbis called qal wahomer: if Scripture, which cannot be broken, calls those to whom God's word came gods, how can it be blasphemy for the one the Father consecrated and sent into the world, the one who is himself the Word (1:1), to call himself the Son of God?

Most interpreters, ancient and modern, conclude that Jesus is not lowering his claim. He immediately says “the Father is in Me, and I am in the Father” (verse 38), his opponents understand him to be repeating the claim and try again to seize him (verse 39), and the Gospel frames the chapter with the confession that the Word was God (1:1) and Thomas's “My Lord and my God” (20:28). On this reading the argument answers the charge on his opponents' own terms from Scripture while pointing beyond it. The church has confessed from the beginning that Jesus is God in the full sense, and that confession belongs to the first order of Christian faith; the debate over Psalm 82's original audience does not change it.

hard.q: Does “no one can snatch them out of My hand” mean a true believer can never fall away?
hard.a:
The Reformed tradition answers yes, and its case is strong. Jesus says his sheep will never perish, that no one can snatch them from his hand or his Father's, and that the Father who gave them is greater than all (verses 28 and 29). Augustine read such promises as the gift of perseverance given to the elect, Calvin's commentary reads them as a guarantee of the elect's salvation, and the Canons of Dort (1619) and the Westminster Confession (1646, chapter 17) teach that those whom God has effectually called can neither totally nor finally fall away. On this view, those who do fall away show that they were never truly among the sheep (compare 1 John 2:19).

Arminian, Wesleyan, Lutheran, Catholic, and Orthodox traditions answer differently, and their case is also serious. They note that the promise is made to sheep who hear and follow (verse 27), described in the present tense of continuing action, and that no outside power can take them, while the text does not address a sheep that stops following. They point to the New Testament's warnings against falling away (Hebrews 6:4-6, John 15:6) and to Judas, who was among those given to Jesus (17:12). Jacob Arminius and the Remonstrants, who in 1610 left the question open, came to hold that a true believer can fall away; John Wesley taught the same, while also teaching a real assurance for those who continue in faith.

This is a second-order question on which faithful churches have long differed, and the text does not settle every part of it. All sides agree on what the verse most plainly teaches: that the security of Christ's sheep rests on the shepherd's hand and the Father's power, not on their own strength, and that the mark of the sheep is that they hear his voice and follow.

observe: List everything the good shepherd does in verses 3 to 4 and 11 to 18. How is it different from what the thief and the hired hand do?
What question do the authorities ask at the Feast of Dedication, and how does Jesus answer it in verses 25 to 30?
What do the people across the Jordan say about John the Baptist and Jesus in verse 41?
interpret: How can Jesus be both the gate and the shepherd? What does each image show about him?
Why do you think Jesus stresses that no one takes his life but that he lays it down of his own accord?
What does the setting of the Feast of Dedication add to Jesus' claim that the Father consecrated him and sent him into the world?
apply: Jesus says his sheep know his voice. How have you learned to recognize his voice from other voices?
The hired hand runs because the sheep aren't his. Where might you be caring for others as a hired hand rather than as someone who belongs to them?
What difference does it make to your sense of security that no one can snatch Jesus' sheep out of his hand?
